messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Modelling categorized, overdispersed count data
parts:
Dear all,

I'm interested in modelling a NB distribution based on overdispersed count data. No problem in itself, except that the count data are categorized (and aggregated) as follows:

  N  count_cat   unit
 y1          0      1
 y2        1-9      1
 y3      10-19      1
 y4        20+      1
 y5          0      2
 y6        1-9      2
 y7      10-19      2
 y8        20+      2

The first column holds the number of obserations of counts within a count category (second column, four categories with known bounds) for a certain hierarchical unit (third column). I want to quantify the underlying NB distribution in terms of mean and overdispersion (at some point in a hierarchical fashion, but not for now). My main question is how to efficiently model this in Stan (in terms of efficient sampling)? I can think of two general approaches:
  1. Use the neg_binomial_2 functions:
    1. Model the zero count category directly using increment_log_prob(y1 * neg_binomial_2_log(0, mu, phi))
    2. Model non-zero count categories using increment_log_prob(y3 * log( neg_binomial_2_cdf(19) - neg_binomial_2_cdf(9) )), which may not be particularly stable (and expensive?) due to the cdf's and the logarithm, right? As a counterpart to the log_sum_exp function, a stable log_min_exp function would be nice here: increment_log_prob(y2 * log_min_exp(neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(9), neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(0))).
  2. Alternatively, use the categorical function, and find a smart way to directly translate the probability density function for a NB distribution to a categorical distribution for count data categories with known bounds. CAVEAT: not sure how stable and efficient the calculations would be. Insights / tips are welcome!

Thanks,

Luc

>
> N count_cat unit
> y1 0 1
> y2 1-9 1
> y3 10-19 1
> y4 20+ 1
> y5 0 2
> y6 1-9 2
> y7 10-19 2
> y8 20+ 2
>
> The first column holds the number of obserations of counts within a count category (second column, four categories with known bounds) for a certain hierarchical unit (third column).

It would be better to use the actual data if you have it,
but I'm going to assume this is all you have.

> I want to quantify the underlying NB distribution in terms of mean and overdispersion (at some point in a hierarchical fashion, but not for now). My main question is how to efficiently model this in Stan (in terms of efficient sampling)? I can think of two general approaches:
> • Use the neg_binomial_2 functions:
> • Model the zero count category directly using increment_log_prob(y1 * neg_binomial_2_log(0, mu, phi))

That's the best thing to do for zero counts.

> • Model non-zero count categories using increment_log_prob(y3 * log( neg_binomial_2_cdf(19) - neg_binomial_2_cdf(9) )), which may not be particularly stable (and expensive?) due to the cdf's and the logarithm, right? ...

The negative binomials are pretty hairy computationally because
they call beta_cdfs, which in turn call various gamma and
digamma functions. But you can always try it and see how stable it
is. This seems like the cleanest approach in terms of being able
to easily read the program.

> • Alternatively, use the categorical function, and find a smart way to directly translate the probability density function for a NB distribution to a categorical distribution for count data categories with known bounds. CAVEAT: not sure how stable and efficient the calculations would be. Insights / tips are welcome!

For this case where you know the sizes are limited, it should be pretty
easy and stable to compute these directly. You can use log_sum_exp
to get the log masses for the 1-9 and 10--19 cases, the 0 case is easy,
and you can use log_1m_exp() to get the remainder, and then do everything
on the logit scale so you can use categorical_logit. Here's some pseudo code:

counts <- c(y1,y2,y3,y4);

lp1 <- nb2_log(0, ...);
lp2 <- log_sum_exp({ nb2_log(1,...), ..., nb2_log(9, ...) });
lp3 <- log_sum_exp({ nb2_log(10,...), ..., nb2_log(19, ...) });
lp4 <- log1m_exp(log_sum_exp({ lp1, lp2, lp3 }));
increment_log_prob(y1 * lp1);
increment_log_prob(y2 * lp2);
increment_log_prob(y3 * lp3);
increment_log_prob(y4 * lp4);

No need to go through categorical() here.

The { ... } notation is meant to indicate array formation.
log1m_exp is another special function.

Not pretty, and it won't be efficient for large ranges, but
should be OK for the actual cases of 1, 1--9, 10--19, and 20+.
> As a counterpart to the log_sum_exp function, a stable log_min_exp function would be nice here: increment_log_prob(y2 * log_min_exp(neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(9), neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(0))).

Feel free to file a feature request. I'd make it log_minus, though, because
"min" confused me at first thinking you meant minimum.

We really do need efficient versions of this for truncated densities.
Right now, we just do the naive thing in the generated code, taking
the log of the difference on the non-log scale.

- Bob
